unit.title: Operate in a culturally diverse work environment

summary: This unit teaches you to work well in a culturally diverse villa or hotel. You will learn what culture and diversity mean, how stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination harm guests and co-workers, how to communicate across cultures and language barriers, and how to meet guests' religious, dietary and access needs without making assumptions. You will also learn how to welcome new colleagues, deal with offence and report unfair treatment.

blocks.p: Jamaica's motto is 'Out of Many, One People'. People of many backgrounds live and work side by side here, and visitors come from all over the world. In a villa or hotel you will serve guests from North America, Europe, Latin America, Asia, Africa and other Caribbean islands, and you will work with colleagues from many families, faiths and parishes. This unit helps you treat every one of them with respect, and make every guest feel at home. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

The unit is not about memorising a list of 'how each nationality behaves'. People from the same country are very different from each other. It is about **attitudes and habits**: asking instead of assuming, listening, speaking simply, being patient and treating everyone fairly.

What this means in a villa or hotel
rows: Explain culture and diversity
Say what culture means and why a diverse team helps a villa
Link it to Jamaica's own mixed heritage
Avoid stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination
Say what each word means and why it harms
Reduce your own bias
Communicate across cultures
Use polite, simple, respectful words and body language
Take care with gestures, eye contact, touch, names and humour
Overcome language barriers
Speak slowly and simply; use pictures, writing and helpers
Check that the guest has understood
Meet religious, dietary and cultural needs
Ask guests about their needs and pass the information on
Respect prayer, fasting, festivals and food rules
Serve guests with different needs
Welcome guests with disabilities, older guests and families
Ask how to help before helping
Work well with colleagues
Welcome new co-workers and respect their dress and customs
Sort out misunderstandings calmly
Deal with offence and unfair treatment
Apologise and put things right
Report discrimination as the policy says

flow: Understand culture
Avoid stereotypes and bias
Communicate across cultures
Overcome language barriers
Meet religious and dietary needs
Serve guests with different needs
Work with colleagues fairly
Put things right and keep learning

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practical tasks you make a welcome kit for guests who speak little English and take part in role plays on cultural needs and misunderstandings. The assessor watches your attitude, your words and your body language as much as the finished work.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Keep practical work respectful. Never mock any real culture, religion or person, and use made-up names on forms.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Culture** is the shared way of life of a group of people: their language, beliefs, customs, food, clothing, music, celebrations, and ideas about manners and family. Everyone has a culture, including you. You may not notice your own, because it feels 'normal'. **Diversity** means that a group contains many different kinds of people. People differ in culture, language, religion, race, age, gender, ability and life experience.

head: What you can see (above the water)
What you cannot see (below the water)
rows: Food and drink
Clothing
Music and dance
Language and greetings
Festivals
Ideas about politeness and respect
Attitudes to time and punctuality
Ideas about personal space and touch
Beliefs about family and roles
Ways of showing feelings or disagreement

blocks.p: Most misunderstandings come from the part below the water. A guest who seems unfriendly may simply have different ideas about politeness. Before you judge, ask yourself: could this be a difference in culture?

Most Jamaicans have African roots. The island's story also includes the Taino people, Europeans, Indian and Chinese workers who came after the end of slavery, and people from the Middle East and many other places. Over time these groups shaped Jamaican food, music, faith and language. Curry goat and roti came with Indian Jamaicans, and Chinese Jamaicans are well known in food and trade. Jamaica's motto, 'Out of Many, One People', says that people can be different and still live and work together as one nation.

blocks.note: You already have an advantage. Jamaicans know from everyday life that differences are normal and can be enjoyed. Use that when you welcome visitors, and be curious and respectful about their cultures, just as you would like visitors to be about ours.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Why a diverse team helps a villa

head: Benefit
Example
rows: Better service
A staff member who speaks Spanish or French helps guests from those countries feel at home
More ideas
People with different experiences solve problems in different ways and suggest ways to please guests
A fairer, happier workplace
When everyone is respected, staff work better together and stay longer
A good name
Guests notice when they and the staff are treated with respect, and tell others

blocks.note: Guests from the same country are not all alike. A guest from Germany may be a retired teacher, a young surfer or a business owner, and each has different needs. Treat each guest as an individual.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: These four words are related, but they are not the same. You must be able to tell them apart.

head: Word
What it means
Workplace example
Why it harms
rows: Stereotype
A fixed, over-simple idea that everyone in a group is the same
'All young guests are noisy.'
Stops you seeing the person in front of you; leads to poor service
Prejudice
Judging a person, often unfairly, before you know them, usually because of a stereotype
Deciding a guest with a strong accent will be difficult before they ask for anything
People feel unwelcome and trust is lost
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of their race, religion, sex, age, disability or background
Giving a co-worker fewer shifts because of their faith; giving a guest slower service
Causes real loss and hurt; breaks the property's rules; can be against the law
Unconscious (hidden) bias
A preference or dislike that you hold without knowing it
Always asking the same person to deal with certain guests without thinking why
It affects your choices even when you mean to be fair

blocks.note: A stereotype can sound like praise ('they are all good at ...') and still be unfair. It treats a person as a type, not as an individual.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Giving a worker fewer shifts or worse tasks because of their religion, race, age or where they come from.
Serving some guests more slowly or less politely because of their accent, dress or nationality.
Refusing to work with, or to serve, a person because of their background.
Making jokes about a person's race, religion, accent or disability.

blocks.h: How to reduce your own bias

flow: Notice your first idea about a person
Ask: is this based on facts or on a stereotype?
Check it against what the person actually says and does
Treat the person as an individual
Learn about other cultures from people themselves
Ask for feedback and correct mistakes

blocks.note: Good service means **the same high standard for every guest**. That does not mean treating everyone identically. It means giving each guest what they need, with the same care, skill and respect.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Villas and hotels have policies on respect, equal opportunity and discrimination, written in the staff handbook or code of conduct. **Equal opportunity** means that every person gets the same fair chance at work, whatever their background. Jamaica also has laws that protect the rights of workers and of people with disabilities. Read your property's policy and follow it. If you are unsure, ask your supervisor.
Good communication is the heart of good service. When guests and colleagues come from different cultures, you must take extra care that your words, your tone and your body language say what you mean.
**Non-verbal communication** is the message you send without words: gestures, facial expressions, eye contact, personal space, touch and tone of voice. It differs between cultures.

head: Signal
What may differ
What you do
rows: Hand gestures
A gesture that is friendly in Jamaica may be rude somewhere else
Use simple, open gestures: a polite nod, an open hand to point instead of one finger
Eye contact
In some cultures looking straight at someone shows honesty; in others, less eye contact shows respect, especially to older people
Do not read a lack of eye contact as rudeness or dishonesty
Personal space
Some guests like to stand close, others like more room
Notice their comfort; step back if they step back
Touch and handshakes
Some people are happy to shake hands or be touched; others, for personal or religious reasons, are not
Let the guest offer a hand first; avoid touching unless needed and ask first
Head movements
A nod means 'yes' in many places, but not in all
Do not rely on a nod alone; check understanding in words or writing
Silence and loudness
Some people speak quietly and pause often; others are loud and fast
Stay calm; do not rush the guest

blocks.note: Speaking louder does not help a person who does not understand you. It only sounds angry. Speak slowly and clearly instead.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Greet every guest warmly with a smile, using 'Good morning' or the guest's own greeting if you know it.
Use the guest's title and surname (for example, 'Mr. Tanaka') until they ask you to use their first name.
In some cultures the family name comes first, so check which part is the family name. If you are not sure how to say a name, **ask politely how to say it**, then use it correctly.
Learn a few greetings in languages common among your guests, such as Spanish, French, German or Portuguese.
Never joke about a person's race, religion, accent, dress or country. A joke that seems harmless may hurt.
Use respectful words for people. Avoid labels. Say 'a guest who uses a wheelchair', not 'a cripple'.
Take care with Jamaican Patois and slang when speaking to visitors. Guests may not understand it, and it can sound as if you are talking about them.
Use friendly, polite words such as 'please' and 'thank you', which are welcome everywhere.

blocks.h: If a guest seems upset by something you said

flow: Notice the guest's reaction and take it seriously
Stay calm; do not argue or defend yourself straight away
Apologise sincerely: 'I am sorry if that upset you'
Listen, and if suitable ask politely what caused the offence
Thank the guest for telling you
Tell your supervisor if the guest is still upset
Learn from it and change what you say next time

blocks.p: An apology does not mean you are admitting that you meant harm. It shows respect for the guest's feelings. It is always better to apologise than to leave the guest upset.

Many guests speak little English, and some Jamaican workers speak Patois more easily than English. Language barriers cause frustration, mistakes and unhappy guests. With patience and a few simple methods, you can usually solve them.

blocks.h: Speaking to a guest who speaks little English

flow: Smile, greet the guest and show you want to help
Speak slowly and clearly, using short, simple words and sentences
Avoid slang, local words, idioms and jokes
Use pictures, gestures, maps, menus with photos and writing
Write down numbers: times, prices and room numbers
Ask a colleague who speaks the language to help
Check understanding by asking the guest to show you or repeat the key point

head: Tool
How it helps
Take care
rows: Gestures and pointing
Shows direction, items and amounts
Use simple, open gestures; a gesture can mean something different elsewhere
Picture cards and photo menus
Guests point to what they need: towels, water, a taxi, a meal
Keep them clean and up to date
Written notes
Times, prices and room numbers are clear in writing
Print clearly; use numerals
Translation app
Helps with key words
May make mistakes; check important points another way
A colleague who speaks the language
Can explain more fully
Ask politely; do not take them away from important work
An interpreter (professional)
Turns spoken words from one language into another
Used for serious matters such as a medical problem or a complaint

blocks.note: Do not rely on a nod or the word 'yes'. A guest may say 'yes' or nod just to be polite. Ask them to show you or repeat the main point: 'Please show me where you would like breakfast.'
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When a colleague's English is learned as a second language

ul: Speak at a steady pace and use plain words.
Listen carefully to their accent. A different accent is not a problem to be corrected.
If you did not understand, say 'Could you say that again, please?' rather than pretending.
Never laugh at the way a person speaks.

blocks.note: Jamaicans often speak English and Patois. Within the team, make sure that nobody is left out of conversations because of language. When a guest is present, speak in a language the guest can follow.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Keep a short list of key phrases and their translations (for example hello, welcome, please, thank you, breakfast, toilet, doctor) in the languages your guests speak. Check them with a reliable source such as a dictionary, an instructor or an app the Centre allows.

The rule is simple: **ask, do not assume**. You cannot tell what a guest eats, believes or needs from their name, dress or country. Ask politely, write the answer down and pass it to everyone who needs to know.

ul: On the booking form and again on arrival: 'Do you have any dietary needs, or anything we can do to make your stay more comfortable?'
Write the answers on the guest record. Tell the cook, the butler and the housekeepers.
Ask again, respectfully, if you are not sure.

head: Need
What it means
What the kitchen must do
rows: Halal
Food allowed under Islamic law. No pork or alcohol, and meat from animals prepared in the required way
Check ingredients and suppliers (including sauces and stock); keep pork and alcohol away from the guest's food
Kosher
Food prepared under Jewish dietary laws. No pork or shellfish, and meat and dairy are kept apart
Ask what the guest needs; do not guess; use sealed kosher food if the guest asks for it
Vegetarian
No meat or fish. Some also avoid eggs or dairy
Ask what the guest eats; use clean pots and utensils
Vegan
No animal foods at all, including eggs, milk, cheese and honey
Check butter, cheese, honey and stock; use separate utensils
No beef or no pork
Some guests avoid certain meats for religious or personal reasons. Many Hindus do not eat beef
Note it; offer other dishes; check mixed dishes
Ital (Rastafari)
Natural, plant-based food, usually with no meat, no processed food and little or no salt
Ask the guest; cook it fresh in clean pots
Allergies
A serious health matter, not a preference
Follow the allergy procedure; never guess; see the food safety unit

blocks.note: Cross-contamination matters. A vegetarian dish cooked in a pot used for meat, or a halal dish served with a spoon used for pork, may not meet the guest's needs. Use clean pots, utensils and boards, and label the food.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Practice
How you can help
rows: Prayer
Many Muslims pray five times a day. Help the guest find a clean, quiet and private space and, if asked, tell them the direction of Mecca if you know it
Fasting
During the month of Ramadan, many Muslims do not eat or drink between dawn and sunset. Ask about meal times, and plan for an early meal before dawn and a meal after sunset
Sabbath or day of rest
Jewish guests keep the Sabbath from Friday evening to Saturday night. Seventh-day Adventists keep it on Saturday. Ask what they need, such as meal arrangements, quiet or fewer requests for signatures
Festivals and holidays
Ask how guests celebrate, and help where suitable, such as a special meal or decorations
Religious dress
Respect it. Do not stare, comment or ask the guest to remove it

blocks.note: Ask politely and never make jokes or comments about a guest's beliefs. Do not ask a guest to explain or defend their religion. If you need to know something for service, ask only that.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Many Jamaicans keep the Sabbath on Saturday, observe Christian holy days and attend church on Sunday. Jamaica also has Muslim, Hindu, Jewish and Rastafari communities. Learning about local communities helps you understand your guests too.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every guest should be able to enjoy their stay. Some guests need a little extra thought: guests with disabilities, older guests, families with young children and guests travelling alone. The golden rule is to **ask how you can help, and listen to the answer**. Do not assume that you know what the person needs.

head: Guest
Good practice
rows: A guest who uses a wheelchair

Speak to the guest, not only to the companion. Ask before helping. Do not touch or lean on the chair. Keep paths clear, and tell the guest about steps, ramps and bathrooms. Offer a seat at table height
A guest who is blind or has low vision
Say who you are as you approach. Describe layouts (for example 'the door is to your left'). Offer your arm if the guest wishes, and walk a little ahead. Tell the guest when you leave
A guest with a guide dog
Welcome both. A guide dog is a working animal: do not pet, feed or distract it. Guide dogs and similar service animals are allowed in guest areas, subject to the property's policy
A guest who is deaf or hard of hearing
Face the guest and speak clearly without shouting. Use writing, gestures and a pen and pad. If the guest uses sign language, ask how best to communicate, or use an interpreter for important matters
A guest with a learning or speech difficulty
Be patient, use simple words, give time and do not finish the guest's sentences

blocks.note: Speak to the guest directly, not to the person who is with them. Use respectful words: 'a guest who uses a wheelchair' rather than 'confined to a wheelchair'.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Walk at the guest's pace and offer help if they want it. Do not rush them.
Offer a chair, clear and well-lit paths, and non-slip surfaces.
Speak clearly and respectfully. Do not talk down to older people or speak to them as to children.
For families, ask about high chairs, cots, child-safe pool areas and food for children.

blocks.note: Safety comes first. Guests with limited movement need clear escape routes. Make sure you know the emergency plan for guests who cannot use the stairs, and tell your supervisor about any guest who may need help leaving the building.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: If a guest asks for different treatment

blocks.p: Sometimes a guest asks for something that is unfair to staff, such as to be served only by people of a certain race, religion or sex. Do not argue and do not agree. Stay polite, say you will pass the request to the manager, and then do exactly that. The manager decides, using the property's policy on equal treatment. In the same way, if a guest makes an offensive remark about a worker, the worker should stay calm, not argue and report it. Staff should not have to accept abuse.

sections.title: Working with colleagues, and putting things right

blocks.p: The way you treat your co-workers matters just as much as the way you treat guests. A team that respects each other serves guests better.

blocks.h: Welcoming a new colleague from another place or background

flow: Greet the new colleague warmly and learn to say their name correctly
Introduce them to the team
Show them the villa: where things are kept, the staff areas, the safety exits and the first-aid kit
Explain how things work: rosters, the log book, house rules and standards
Use clear, simple words and check that they understand
Include them in breaks, conversations and team activities
Help them speak to the supervisor about any needs, such as prayer times or a special diet
Check how they are getting on after the first week

ul: Accept religious dress and symbols, as long as they meet the property's safety and hygiene rules. For example, a headscarf is fine in a kitchen if it covers the hair safely.
Respect different days of rest and festivals when making the roster, where it is fair and possible.
Do not make comments or jokes about a colleague's accent, food, dress or beliefs.
Be patient while a new colleague learns local ways and words. Do not make fun of mistakes.
Do not gossip about colleagues' backgrounds.

flow: Stay calm and do not assume the worst
Speak in private, at a good time
Explain what you meant and how it felt, using 'I' statements
Listen to the other person without interrupting
Agree what each of you will do
Ask the supervisor to help if it carries on

blocks.p: Many conflicts between colleagues of different backgrounds start with a simple misunderstanding. For example, one person may think another is rude because they do not look them in the eye, when in fact it is a sign of respect in their culture.

If you see a colleague treat a guest or another worker unfairly because of their background, that is discrimination. It breaks the property's rules, can be against the law and damages the villa's good name.

flow: Make sure the guest or worker gets proper service or help, without a scene
Do not join in, laugh or ignore it
If it is safe, speak to the colleague privately afterwards
Report it to your supervisor with the facts: what, when, where and who saw it
Keep it confidential; do not gossip
Follow the policy; the supervisor decides the next steps

blocks.note: Report the facts only. Do not guess at motives. 'I heard Mr. Smith say that guests from that country are lazy' is a clear report; 'He hates foreigners' is a guess.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Think about your own culture and habits. Realise that your way is not the only way.
Ask respectful questions and listen to people's stories.
Learn a few greetings and phrases in other languages.
Read, watch and take part in training on diversity and customer service.
Ask your supervisor and colleagues for feedback.
When you make a mistake, apologise, learn from it and change.
I can say what culture and cultural diversity mean, and give three benefits of a diverse team.
I can link Jamaica's motto 'Out of Many, One People' to welcoming visitors.
I can explain stereotype, prejudice, discrimination and unconscious bias, with examples.
I can say how to reduce my own bias.
I can use non-verbal communication with care: gestures, eye contact, touch and personal space.
I can ask how to say a guest's name and use it correctly.
I can speak to a guest who speaks little English, using simple words, pictures and writing.
I can check that a guest has understood.
I can say what halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan and ital mean, and how to avoid cross-contamination.
I can help guests who need to pray, fast or keep a day of rest.
I can serve guests with disabilities and older guests politely and safely.
I can welcome a new colleague and respect their dress, language and customs.
I can apologise and put things right when a guest is offended.
I can report discrimination to my supervisor with the facts, as the policy says.
I can say where to find my workplace's rules on respect and discrimination.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason as well as the action. For example: 'I ask the guest about their diet instead of guessing, because people from the same country can have very different needs.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The shared language, beliefs, customs, food and way of life of a group of people.
Having many different kinds of people in the same group.
A fixed idea that everyone in a group is the same.
Judging someone unfairly before you know them.
Treating someone unfairly because of their race, religion, sex, age, disability or background.
A hidden preference that you hold without knowing it.
The principle that everyone gets the same fair chance at work.
Accepting and respecting beliefs or customs different from your own.
Being aware of other cultures and avoiding words or actions that may offend.
Communication without words, such as gestures, eye contact and facial expressions.
The area around a person's body that they feel is their own.
A person who turns spoken words from one language into another.
Food prepared under Jewish dietary laws.
A person who eats no meat or fish, but may eat eggs and milk.
A person who eats no animal foods at all.
Natural, plant-based food eaten by many Rastafari.
Passing something unwanted, such as meat or an allergen, from one food or tool to another.
A trained dog that helps a person who is blind to move around safely.
The property's written rules on how staff must behave.

c1.title: A Japanese couple at a Port Antonio villa
c1.text: Mr. Hiroshi Tanaka and his wife are staying for a week at a villa in Port Antonio. They speak a little English. On arrival the couple take off their shoes at the door and look around for somewhere to put them. Trainee Camille is not sure which name to use when she greets Mr. Tanaka, and the booking form lists him as 'Tanaka Hiroshi'. At breakfast the next day, Mr. Tanaka asks about 'the bus for the market', and Camille isn't sure that he has understood her directions.

c2.title: A Sabbath weekend in Montego Bay
c2.text: A family of six are guests at a villa in Montego Bay for a long weekend. On Thursday the father, Mr. Cohen, tells the butler, Marlon, that the family keep the Sabbath from Friday evening to Saturday night. He asks whether the dining room and corridor lights can be left on, and whether the family can be spared requests to sign forms or pay on Saturday. Marlon has never worked with guests who keep the Sabbath.

c3.title: A vegetarian wedding party in Mandeville
c3.text: A Hindu family have booked a villa in Mandeville for a small wedding celebration with 30 guests. The bride's mother tells the cook, Miss Hyacinth, that most of the family are vegetarian and that none of them eat beef. The villa's kitchen is small and the same pots are used for meat dishes. A young kitchen helper, Orane, says, 'Hindus do not eat any meat, so just don't cook meat that day.'

c4.title: A new colleague at a Kingston guest house
c4.text: Rosa, from Colombia, has just joined the front desk team of a guest house in Kingston. Spanish is her first language and she speaks careful English with an accent. On her second day, another worker, Mr. Bryan, laughs at the way she says 'water' and mimics her in front of two guests. Rosa goes quiet. Later, she asks the supervisor if she may pray for five minutes in a quiet room during her afternoon break.

c5.title: A wheelchair user at an Ocho Rios villa
c5.text: Mr. Anthony Gordon, who uses a wheelchair, is staying at a villa in Ocho Rios with his daughter. The villa has a ramp at the front door but two steps at the pool terrace. When Mr. Gordon arrives, trainee Shanice speaks only to his daughter and asks her where he would like his bags put. Later, Mr. Gordon says he would like to sit by the pool in the afternoon.

questions.q: What is the best way for Camille to find out how to address Mr. Tanaka?
o: Call him 'Hiroshi', because the booking form lists that as his first name
Ask him politely which name he prefers and how to say it
Use a nickname, so that the greeting sounds more friendly and relaxed
Avoid using his name at all until he tells her what it is at breakfast
questions.why: In some cultures the family name comes first, so the order on a form can mislead. Asking politely, then using the name correctly, shows respect.

questions.q: The couple take off their shoes at the door. What should Camille do?
o: Offer a place for the shoes and perhaps slippers, and respect their custom
Tell them that shoes may stay on in a Jamaican villa and ask them to put them back on
Say nothing and leave the shoes in the middle of the doorway for anyone to trip on
Ask them why they do this and whether it is a religious rule they must follow
questions.why: Removing shoes indoors is a common custom in many places. A respectful host makes it easy, for example by providing a rack or slippers, and does not question or discourage it.

questions.q: How should Camille check that Mr. Tanaka has understood the directions to the market?
o: Repeat the same directions louder and nod until he nods back
Say 'Do you understand?' and accept it if he says yes
Tell him it is easy to find and that he will work it out when he gets there
Write the bus number and time down, and ask him to repeat the main points
questions.why: A guest may nod or say yes to be polite. Writing key details and asking the guest to repeat or show you checks real understanding.

questions.q: Which of these is the most suitable way to give directions to the Tanakas?
o: A fast explanation in Patois, since the guests are in Jamaica and should learn it
Long, detailed sentences, so that every turn is included in the explanation
Short, plain sentences, with a simple map or pictures and no slang
Telling them to ask someone in town because the directions are too hard to explain
questions.why: Simple words, a map or pictures and no slang or Patois give a guest with limited English the best chance of understanding.

questions.q: What should Marlon do first about the Cohens' requests?
o: Tell Mr. Cohen that the villa cannot change anything for religious reasons
Say yes, then forget to tell the housekeepers and the cook about the request
Thank him, ask what else the family needs, and tell the team
Ask Mr. Cohen to explain his religion to him in detail before he does anything
questions.why: Ask what the guest needs, record it and pass it on so that the whole team can help. Refusing without checking, forgetting to share the request, or asking for a long explanation is poor service.

questions.q: Which step would best help the Cohens on Saturday?
o: Ask them to sign the bill during breakfast on Saturday as with any other guest
Settle forms and the bill on Friday, and arrange meals and lights
Switch off the corridor lights at night as the villa does for every other guest
Send housekeeping to knock on their door each hour to ask whether they need help
questions.why: Planning ahead, such as settling forms and the bill on Friday, lets the family keep their day of rest. Following the usual routine, or frequent interruptions, would ignore their request.

questions.q: Which comment would be disrespectful and must never be made?
o: 'You people have such strange rules; why can't you just relax them while you are here?'
'Please let me know if there is anything else we can do to make your stay comfortable'
'Thank you for telling me. I will pass this on to the cook and to the housekeepers today'
'Is there anything else the family would like us to arrange for the long weekend?'
questions.why: Comments or jokes about a guest's beliefs are never acceptable. The other options show willingness to help and respect.

questions.q: What should Miss Hyacinth do about Orane's comment?
o: Agree with Orane, because all Hindus are strict vegetarians who eat no animal products
Ignore it, because the bride's mother has already said what is needed
Tell Orane to repeat it to the guests in case any of them are not vegetarian
Say that practice varies, and ask the family exactly what they eat
questions.why: Not every member of a faith follows the same practice. Orane's idea is a stereotype. The right step is to ask the family, not to assume.

questions.q: How should the cook prepare the vegetarian dishes in the small kitchen?
o: Cook them in the same pots as the meat dishes, after a quick rinse with water
Cook them first in the meat pots, so that the flavour is richer and more authentic
Use the pots from the meat dishes, but serve with a clean spoon on the day
Use clean pots, spoons and boards that have not touched meat, and label the dishes
questions.why: Meat left in pots or on utensils can contaminate a vegetarian dish and break the guests' dietary rules. Separate, clean equipment and labels avoid this.

questions.q: One dish is a mixed rice and vegetable dish made with a beef stock cube. What should the cook do?
o: Use the beef stock, as there is no actual beef meat in the dish
Use half the stock cube to reduce the beef flavour
Use a vegetable stock instead, as the family eat no beef
Serve it as planned without telling the guests how it was made
questions.why: Hidden ingredients such as stock still mean the guests are eating beef. Check every ingredient, including stock, sauces and seasonings.

questions.q: A guest later asks whether the dessert contains egg. The cook is not sure. What is the best response?
o: Say that it does not, to avoid any worry before the wedding
Check the recipe first, then give an honest answer
Say 'probably not' and carry on serving the dessert
Tell the guest to ask somebody else at the villa
questions.why: Never guess about ingredients. A wrong answer could break a guest's dietary rules or, with an allergy, harm health. Check, then answer honestly.

questions.q: What was wrong with Mr. Bryan's behaviour?
o: He mocked a colleague's accent in front of guests
He spoke to a guest about the weather without checking that Rosa agreed
He made a friendly joke, which is fine as long as nobody is badly hurt
He corrected Rosa's pronunciation to help her learn better English
questions.why: Mocking a person's accent is disrespectful and can be a form of discrimination. It makes the person feel unwelcome and gives guests a poor impression.

questions.q: What should Rosa's supervisor do when Rosa asks to pray during her break?
o: Agree to a quiet room during her break, if the work allows
Refuse, because the guest house does not allow staff to do anything private
Say that she may pray only if she makes up the time at the end of the day
Tell Rosa to find another job if she cannot work without extra breaks
questions.why: Respecting religious practice, within the property's rules and the needs of the work, helps a colleague feel valued. Praying in a break does not stop work.

questions.q: Which action by a colleague best helps Rosa after what happened?
o: Join in the laughter, to avoid being left out of the group
Say nothing, since it will be forgotten by next week anyway
Tell the guests that Rosa is new and has not learned English yet
Check on Rosa and tell the supervisor what Mr. Bryan did
questions.why: Supporting Rosa and reporting the behaviour helps to stop it from happening again. Joining in, staying silent or drawing attention to her makes it worse.

questions.q: How should Mr. Bryan's supervisor deal with this?
o: Laugh it off, because it was only a bit of fun among workmates
Tell all the guests about it as an example of staff problems
Speak to him privately and follow the property's policy
Make Rosa speak to Mr. Bryan alone without anyone else being present
questions.why: The supervisor should deal with it fairly and privately under the policy, so that the behaviour stops and Rosa is protected.

questions.q: What did Shanice do wrong when Mr. Gordon arrived?
o: She offered to carry his bags as soon as the family arrived
She spoke to his daughter, not to him
She told him about the ramp at the front door of the villa
She greeted him with a smile and her own name on arrival
questions.why: A guest who uses a wheelchair should be spoken to directly and asked what they want. Speaking only to a companion is disrespectful.

questions.q: The pool terrace has two steps. What is the best action?
o: Tell him that the pool is not suitable for him and suggest he stay in his room
Ask how he would like to get there and arrange a ramp
Lift him in his chair down the steps straight away without asking
Say nothing and leave him to find a way when he is ready
questions.why: Ask first, and arrange safe, suitable access. Assuming he cannot use the pool, or lifting him unasked, takes away his choice and may be unsafe.

questions.q: If Mr. Gordon asks for help to move his chair over the grass, what should Shanice do?
o: Ask how he would like her to help, then do exactly that
Push the chair at once and as fast as she can across the lawn
Lean on the chair to steady herself while she carries the bags
Tell him that the grass is too hard to cross and that he should stay in the room
questions.why: Always ask how to help. A wheelchair is part of the person's personal space, and the way to move it safely differs from person to person.

questions.q: Why should a guest's dietary and religious needs be written on the guest record and shared with the team?
o: So that the villa can charge extra for any special meal or service that is requested
So that the manager can decide whether the guest's request is reasonable or not
So that guests with similar needs can be placed in the same rooms at the villa
So that every team member can meet the need without asking again and again
questions.why: A written, shared record means the cook, butler and housekeepers all know what the guest needs, and the guest does not have to repeat it at every meal and every visit.

questions.q: Which statement about stereotypes is correct?
o: They are harmless as long as the idea is positive and well-meant
They are accurate when a lot of people from a group behave in the same way
They treat a person as a type, even when the idea sounds like a compliment
They save time because guests from the same country always want the same things
questions.why: Even a 'positive' stereotype ignores the individual and can lead to unfair or poor service. Asking each guest what they need is better.
